blocks.content: Have you ever written a line of code that looked like this?
school.getDepartment().getTeacher().getSubject().getGrade();
One line. Four dots. Four different classes chained together. It works. It compiles. But the moment any one of those classes changes, everything breaks.
This is a violation of one of the most overlooked principles in software design: The Law of Demeter.
1. The Problem
Let's say you are building a school management system. You have:
["A School that has a Department","The department has a Teacher","The teacher has a Subject","The subject has a Grade"]
Now you want to find the grade of a subject taught in a department. A common but flawed approach looks like this:
Grade grade = school.getDepartment().getTeacher().getSubject().getGrade();

Look at that chain. The ReportService now knows about the school's department, the department's teacher, the teacher's subject, and the subject's grade. It is reaching deep into four different classes just to get one piece of information.
Here is the full function using this pattern:

This works today. But tomorrow, if Teacher is restructured or Subject changes how it stores grades, this single line breaks. And ReportService has absolutely nothing to do with how teachers or subjects are structured internally.
This is called a train wreck. One object reaching through several others just to get what it wants. And it is a problem that grows silently until something breaks at the worst possible time.
2. What Is Wrong With This?
1. High Coupling
The ReportService is now tightly coupled to the entire internal structure of the school.
["If Department changes how it stores teachers","If Teacher renames its getSubject() method","If Subject evolves to store grades differently"]
Your ReportService breaks. Even though it had absolutely nothing to do with any of those decisions.
2. Encapsulation Violation
You are reaching deep into the internals of every object in the chain.
["School exposes its Department","Department exposes its Teacher","Teacher exposes its Subject","Subject exposes its Grade"]
Every dot in that chain is a wall being torn down. Encapsulation exists to hide these internal details. This code ignores that completely.
3. Maintenance Nightmare

Imagine Grade changes from storing a letter like "A" to storing a numeric value like 90. Now every single place in your codebase that chained its way to getGrade() needs to be found and updated manually. Miss one and you have a bug.
4. Testability Issues
Testing displaySubjectGrade() becomes a mocking nightmare. To test this one function in isolation you need to mock:
["A School that returns a Department","A Department that returns a Teacher","A Teacher that returns a Subject","A Subject that returns a Grade"]
One function. Four mocks. That is a clear sign something is wrong with the design.
3. The Law of Demeter
"Only talk to your immediate friends." Law of Demeter
The Law of Demeter was created in 1987 at Northeastern University. The idea is simple. A method should only talk to the objects closest to it. Not to the friends of friends of friends.
In plain terms: do not reach through one object to get to another.
A method should only call:
["Itself","Its own fields","Its method parameters","Objects it creates"]
If you write a.getB().getC().doSomething() you are violating LoD. You are reaching through B to talk to C. You should only talk to A and let A figure out the rest.
4. Fixing It Step by Step
The strategy is simple. Push the responsibility down to the class that owns the data. Each class exposes a meaningful method instead of exposing its internals.
Step 1: Add a method to Department
Department owns its teachers. So it should answer questions about them.
Step 2: Add a method to School
School owns the Department. So it should delegate department related questions.
Step 3: Update ReportService
Now ReportService only talks to its direct friend: School.
Before the fix `ReportService` was reaching through four objects to get one value. Now it asks `School` for what it needs and `School` handles the rest internally.

Before: ReportService→School→Department→Teacher→Subject→Grade
After: ReportService→School
ReportService no longer cares how departments store teachers, how teachers store subjects, or how subjects store grades. It just asks and gets an answer.
That is the Law of Demeter at work.
4. Benefits of Law of Demeter
Low Coupling
Each class only depends on its immediate neighbor. When Department changes how it stores teachers internally, only Department needs updating. ReportService does not even notice.
Better Encapsulation
Objects expose meaningful behavior instead of raw internals. Instead of saying "give me your list so I can dig through it", you say "give me the grade" and the object figures out the rest.
Easier Refactoring
You can change internal implementations without touching consumers. If Subject changes how it stores grades, only Teacherand Department need to adapt. ReportService stays completely untouched.
Improved Testability
Fewer mocks needed. Instead of mocking six layers just to test one function, you mock one object and get your answer. Clean, fast, simple tests.
Cleaner APIs
Public methods become meaningful and intentional. Callers get clear entry points that describe exactly what they want instead of navigating a maze of objects.
5. Common Questions About LoD
Is this not just more code?

Yes, you write a few extra delegating methods. But think of it this way: would you rather write three lines now to isolate behavior, or refactor three hundred lines later when your system breaks? These small wrappers protect your entire codebase from internal changes.
Does LoD mean no getters at all?
No. Simple property access is perfectly fine.
school.getName() // perfectly fine
The problem is chained getters crossing object boundaries.
school.getDepartment().getTeacher().getSubject().getGrade() // violation
The deeper the chain, the tighter the coupling.
What about data structures like List or Map?
Calling simple operations on standard collections is generally acceptable.
school.getTeachers().size() // acceptable
But traversing domain objects through that collection is a violation.
school.getTeachers().get(0).getSubject().getGrade() // violation
The more domain objects you cross, the worse it gets.
When is it okay to break LoD?
LoD is a guideline, not a law carved in stone. Some acceptable exceptions are:

["DTOs and Value Objects: Simple data carriers with no real behavior are fine to traverse.","Stable Libraries: Using List.size() or Map.get() is safe and expected.","Fluent Builders: Method chaining in builder patterns is intentional design, not a violation."]
items: DTOs and Value Objects: Simple data carriers with no real behavior are fine to traverse.
Fluent Builders: Method chaining in builder patterns is intentional design, not a violation.

blocks.content: The key word is intentional. If you understand the trade-off and it makes sense, go ahead. Just never do it by accident.
LoD is not about writing perfect code. It is about avoiding the slow, painful trap of tying your entire system together through hidden chains of dependency. Talk to your friends. Not to strangers.
6. Practical Example: Library Book Return Notification
blocks.text: 6. Practical Example: Library Book Return Notification

blocks.content: Let's look at another scenario. We are building a notification system for a library app. The NotificationService needs three pieces of information to send a return reminder:
["The member's name from their profile","The book title from the book details","The member's phone number from their contact info"]
items: The member's name from their profile
The book title from the book details
The member's phone number from their contact info

blocks.content: The Problem
A developer in a hurry writes this:
`NotificationService` now knows about `Member`,`Profile`,`Book`,`BookDetails`,and `ContactInfo`.Every internal change in any of these classes is a potential breaking point.
The Fix: Delegation Methods

Instead of letting NotificationService dig through the entire object graph, we add delegation methods to Booking. Bookingalready has references to Guest and Room, so it is the natural place to answer these questions.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245770982-1f726735.png
Step 1: Add delegation methods to Booking
Step 2: SimplifyNotificationService
7. Why This Works
Single point of change. If Room restructures how it stores room numbers, you update Booking.getRoomNumber() only. Nothing else breaks.
Easy to test. To test NotificationService you only mock Booking with three simple return values. No chain of mocks needed.
Self documenting. Method names like getGuestName() and getRoomNumber() clearly describe what is being retrieved without exposing how it is obtained.
Contained ripple effects. Internal changes inside Guest, Room, or ContactInfo stay contained within the classes that own them.
